title: Satnam on the breath
hookLine: Sat on the inhale, Nam on the exhale

lines: MANY NAMES FOR ONE YOU LOVE.
cards: The people you love tend to have more than one name. The full name on the birth certificate. The nickname.
The name only you use. Each one holds something different. The Guru Granth Sahib is like that about God.
It uses many names, from many languages: Hari, Ram, Allah, Gobind, Prabhu, Kartar. But in the book's very first line there's a name that isn't really a name at all. It's a description.
Two syllables, and it fits a breath exactly.

teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mul Mantar, the root verse. It begins with Ik Onkar, there is one God. The very next word is Satnam.
Sat means true, real, what lasts. Nam means name.
So Satnam is the true name, or better, the one whose name is truth. Here's the quiet surprise.

teach.h: A QUALITY, NOT A PROPER NAME.
teach.b: Guru Nanak doesn't give God a proper name here. He gives a quality. Right after saying God is one, the text says God is real.
Not a rumor, not a mood. True. Sikhs don't treat Satnam as a different God or a secret password.
It's a way of naming the same One by what never changes.
That's why it works so well as simran. Sat on the in-breath: the real, coming in.

teach.h: THE ONE WHOSE NAME IS TRUTH.
teach.b: Nam on the out-breath: the name, going out into the day. Many Sikhs use Waheguru for simran, since that's the Gurmantar; some also breathe with Satnam, or say Satnam Waheguru together.
Practices differ from sangat to sangat, and both words appear in the Guru Granth Sahib. You may have heard Satnam used as a greeting, or in yoga classes in the West.

The everyday Sikh greeting is something else, Sat Sri Akal, but sat is in there too. Truth keeps turning up. Elsewhere in the Granth, Guru Nanak says truth is high, but higher still is truthful living.
Satnam on the breath starts there: one real thing, noticed, again and again.

how: Satnam, from the opening line of the Guru Granth Sahib, is repeated in simran by some Sikhs, sometimes with Sat on the in-breath and Nam on the out-breath, and sometimes together with Waheguru.

o: God named by a quality: truth
a secret name given at baptism

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: Satnam is the name of a separate god
it's a way of naming the one God by a quality: truth.
Satnam comes right after Ik Onkar at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib
it's in the Mul Mantar, the book's opening root verse.
the everyday Sikh greeting is Satnam
the everyday greeting is Sat Sri Akal, though sat, true, is in it too.

games.q: the Guru Granth Sahib is about to name God for the first time. what comes right after one God?
o: a proper name, like Ram or Allah.
games.why: Satnam. before any proper name, God is described as true, the one whose name is truth.

practice: Ten breaths again, with the new word: let your shoulders drop, think Sat for the whole in-breath, and Nam all the way out.
If you pray, let it be prayer; if you're here to learn, hear it as a plain word, true, name, and notice whether it feels different from yesterday's Wahe and Guru. Then just breathe.

wordCard.voice: Satnam. Sat is true, Nam is name: the one whose name is truth, right after Ik Onkar at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, from the Mul Mantar: the true name, or the one whose name is truth.

carryVoice: Your line: true name, breathing. Sat on the way in, Nam on the way out. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Raag, Ang 62 (truth is high, higher still is truthful living)
